tier_reason: results/README.md gives the timings with GNU 7.4.0, Ubuntu 18.04 and the CPU model (Xeon E5-1660 v4, turbo off, performance governor); the benchmark code is public (benchmark.cpp, functions.cpp) and CMakeLists.txt states the flags (-std=c++11 -Wall -pthread -march=native, CMake Release build).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GNU 7.4.0; CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS '-std=c++11 -Wall -pthread -march=native -lm' and the README builds with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's default Release flags for GCC add -O3 -DNDEBUG)
corrections.caveats: No LICENSE file (none in the top-level listing, and the GitHub sidebar shows no license), so usability is reference; Philox.h and PhiloxSIMD.h say the engine was 'Originally implemented in PyTorch's fusion compiler' (PyTorch is BSD-3-Clause), but the repo itself grants nothing. PhiloxSIMD.h defaults to UNSHUFFLE 0, which skips the transpose ('set to 1 to match non-SIMD ordering'), so the benchmarked SIMD stream is a block-wise reordering of standard Philox4x32-10 output and the timings exclude the cost of restoring standard order. The SIMD variants consume outputs with vector adds while scalar engines are called one value at a time. Counts are in 32-bit units for every engine (64-bit engines count two per call), so the comparison is per bit. At tiny counts (8 numbers) xoshiro256** is faster (1.58e-7 s vs 1.79e-7 s). 2019 results on GCC 7.4, single machine.

notes: All quoted 1-thread numbers match results/README.md exactly (philox_simd global 0.176079 s, thread local 0.187869 s, xoshiro256** 0.650694 s, pcg64 0.65864 s, std::mt19937 1.60893 s, at::mt19937 0.392547 s, philox 0.438846 s). baseline_stdlib set to libstdc++ because the only compiler is GNU 7.4.0 on Ubuntu. 4 stars, last commit 2019-07-18, no license confirmed.

tier_reason: README charts state OS, compiler version, CPU model, SIMD target and Eigen version per platform; the benchmark code is public (benchmark/benchmark.cpp, std::mt19937_64 plus std distributions as reference) and the build is public: CMakeLists.txt Release flags (-O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC/Clang, -O2 -Oi -Gy for MSVC) plus the target flag passed by .github/workflows/release.yml (-mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 for the AVX2 runs).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '5~10 times faster than non-vectorized functions'. Charts (speed-up over the std or Eigen reference, read by eye, approximate): Ubuntu GCC 7.5 AVX2 on Xeon Platinum 8370C: uniformReal about 22x, normal(0,1) about 8x, uniformInt(0~63) about 10x, cauchy about 15x, binomial(20,0.5) about 24x, discrete(fp32) about 32x, several only about 1.6x-1.7x (chiSquared, gamma(10.5,1), fisherF(5,5), uniformInt(0~100k)). Windows MSVC 19.29 AVX2 on Xeon Platinum 8171M: about 3x-61x (uniformReal about 61x, gamma(5,3) about 33x, randBits about 3x). macOS clang 13.1.6 NEON on Apple M1 Pro: about 1.1x-15x, but binomial(100,0.75) (about 0.6x) and weibull (about 0.75x) are slower than the reference (orange bars).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ubuntu 18.04 GCC 7.5.0 AVX2; Windows MSVC 19.29.30147 AVX2; macOS Monterey Apple clang 13.1.6 NEON; Eigen 3.4.0. CMakeLists.txt Release flags: -DNDEBUG -DRELEASE -O3 plus EIGENRAND_CXX_FLAGS on GCC/Clang, -DNDEBUG -DRELEASE -O2 -Oi -Gy on MSVC; the CI benchmark workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) passes -mavx2 (Linux) or /arch:AVX2 (Windows) for its AVX2 matrix entries. The workflow at HEAD runs on ubuntu-22.04/24.04 and windows-2022, so the exact 2022-era chart runs are not reproducible from the current file verbatim.
corrections.caveats: Charts are bar images (values read by eye); the exact numbers are on GitHub Actions run pages that were not opened. The chart machines (Xeon Platinum 8370C/8171M) are shared CI runners, so noise is likely. Speed-ups range from about 0.6x to about 61x depending on distribution and platform; on Apple M1 Pro NEON binomial(100,0.75) and weibull are slower than the std reference. The std reference is std::mt19937_64 plus the std distribution, which is not vectorizable; EigenRand also offers a vectorized engine (Vmt19937_64). Charts use Eigen 3.4.0; current code supports Eigen 5.0.x.

notes: Ubuntu chart values in the record match; added the Windows and macOS charts, which include two NEON regressions. MIT, 105 stars, last commit 2026-03-17, latest release 0.6.0 (2026-01-31). baseline_stdlib (libstdc++, MSVC STL, libc++) matches the three charted toolchains.

tier_reason: The README tables (also in result/Corei5-3330S@2.70GHz_mac64_clang6.1.csv) come from public benchmark code (src/*.cpp, cpp11random = std::normal_distribution with std::minstd_rand); the CPU (Core i5-3330S) is stated, the compiler (clang 6.1, mac64) is named in the linked result file, and build/premake4.lua gives the flags.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 6.1 on macOS 64-bit (named in the result file Corei5-3330S@2.70GHz_mac64_clang6.1 linked from the README); build/premake4.lua release config: premake4 'Optimize' flag (-O2) with NDEBUG, plus -mavx -Wall -Wextra -std=c++11 for gmake
corrections.license: MIT (src/ziggurat.cpp is Jochen Voss's GPL-2.0-or-later code)
corrections.caveats: Not a like-for-like comparison: cpp11random pays for std::minstd_rand plus the library's normal_distribution, while the other implementations use the 'simplest' LCG, so part of the gap is the cheaper, lower-quality uniform source. The README's Speedup column for float is relative to clt16, not to cpp11random; the ratios against std are derived from page data. CLT variants fail the repo's own kurtosis check. src/ziggurat.cpp is GPL-2.0-or-later (Jochen Voss, 2005) inside an MIT repo, so the ziggurat code carries copyleft terms. Single 2012-era CPU and a 2015 toolchain; repo unchanged since 2015-07-10.

notes: All numbers match the README and the result CSV (float: cpp11random 18.642 ns, boxmuller_avx 2.253, boxmuller_sse2 3.752, ziggurat 6.731; double: cpp11random 32.245, ziggurat 7.086). baseline_stdlib set to libc++ on the inference that Apple clang on macOS links libc++ by default (premake4.lua sets no -stdlib). The README file is readme.md (lowercase).
